claims.text: A combined high-throughput calorimetry and CALPHAD approach can reliably determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad spectrum of high-entropy alloys.
Homogenization minimizes compositional gradients in polycrystalline high-entropy alloy samples.
High-throughput DSC or drop calorimetry can be used in tandem with CALPHAD modeling across high-entropy-alloy composition space.
The proposed measurements can be conducted over 300–1800 K in inert atmospheres.
CALPHAD parameters can be validated against known phase equilibria and thermochemical reference data for simpler alloys.
Multiple principal elements produce a large configurational entropy in high-entropy alloys.
Partial local ordering influences high-entropy-alloy melting behavior and thermodynamics.
Variations in mixing enthalpy influence high-entropy-alloy melting behavior and thermodynamics.
Combining calorimetry with validated thermodynamic models captures intrinsic multicomponent entropy contributions.
Combining calorimetry with validated thermodynamic models captures enthalpic interactions among constituent elements.
Capturing multicomponent entropy and enthalpic interactions enables accurate thermodynamic-property predictions across diverse high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The combined approach will achieve average melting-temperature uncertainties below ±10 K.
The combined approach will achieve enthalpy-of-fusion uncertainties of ±5–10%.
The combined approach will achieve entropy-of-fusion uncertainties of ±5–10%.
Predicted volume changes at melting will agree with reference dilatometry data within ±0.3%.
Single-method approaches can have melting-temperature uncertainties exceeding ±30 K for multicomponent alloys.
Single-method approaches can have enthalpy- or entropy-of-fusion uncertainties exceeding ±15–20% for multicomponent alloys.
The approach is most accurate for near-homogeneous solid-solution high-entropy alloys containing at least five principal components.
Alloys with significant short-range ordering or intermetallic phases require improved experimental calibration and computational databases.
Incomplete or oversimplified thermodynamic descriptions can cause computed and measured results to diverge, especially in segregated or kinetically constrained systems.
